paras: The attempted lynching of Leroy Gibbons took place in east Georgia in late May 1903, when white men searching for a missing white farmer, Dupree Holmes, seized Gibbons, an elderly Black man accused of killing him, and whipped his wife until she named him as the killer. Gibbons broke away and surrendered to the sheriff, and Holmes came home alive on May 31, saying he had been ill at a sawmill. Early wire reports said Gibbons had probably been lynched; after Holmes reappeared, Georgia papers and the Black press cited the case against mob law.

Holmes, a young man from a well-known family, left home on Tuesday, May 26, to collect money Gibbons owed him. His horse came home that afternoon without him, and he could not be traced beyond Gibbons's house. Reports placed the affair at Matthews in Jefferson County (Augusta), in the Stellaville district of Burke County (Louisville), or, for the arrests, at Blitch in Bulloch County (Associated Press).

On Thursday, May 28, men went to Gibbons's home to demand what had become of Holmes, and Gibbons said he had not seen him. The men then whipped his wife, who said under the lash that her husband had killed Holmes with a hoe and thrown the body in Briar Creek. According to the Louisville dispatch, friends of Holmes overpowered his guard at Stellaville and took him to the swamp, where "a rope was put about his neck to bring out the truth of the matter."

Gibbons protested his innocence, broke away from the men into the swamp, and made his way to Louisville, where he surrendered to the Jefferson County sheriff. Black residents, believing he had been lynched, "became very indignant," and Sheriff Farmer went to Stellaville with a deputy. The sheriff then sent Gibbons to the jail at Macon for his safety.

While searchers dragged Briar Creek, Holmes walked into his home uninjured on the morning of May 31. He said he had fallen sick at a sawmill about ten miles away and stayed there unaware of the search, an account the Augusta correspondent said had "strange features." The sheriff wired that Gibbons be released at Macon and given transportation home.

Gibbons's wife, "beaten almost insensible," was in a very precarious condition and said she believed she would have been killed had she not accused her husband. No report of arrests or prosecution of the men involved appears in the coverage.

The first Associated Press reports of May 29 treated Gibbons as the killer, with the Brunswick Daily News headlining "Has Probably Been Lynched" and the Richmond Times-Dispatch "Confessed That His Father Is Murderer." The Raleigh News & Observer carried the same dispatch, and the Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger still printed it on June 5, after Holmes had come home. In Georgia, the Brunswick Daily News and the Atlanta Constitution reported that Gibbons "Really Escaped," and digest columns such as the Americus Times-Recorder's noted Holmes's return.

The Savannah Morning News headlined its fullest account "Lied Under the Lash" and called Gibbons "a peaceable old negro" and "an innocent man." Its June 2 editorial argued that "the law should be permitted to take its course on all occasions," while allowing that the searchers would have "profoundly regretted" a lynching. The Deseret Evening News of Salt Lake City retold the story on June 15 as evidence that lynchers' claims to justice were "miserable pretenses," calling the attackers "a band of white ruffians."

The Black weekly Plaindealer took up the case on June 12 as "The Danger of Lynching," stating that "Gibbons is a Negro" and that his wife was whipped "in the brutal hope that she would make a confession." Where the Savannah editorial noted the searchers' regret, the Plaindealer stressed "the outrage and danger of mob rule."

Accounts differ on who implicated Gibbons: most name his wife, under the lash, while the first Associated Press dispatch said his son confessed and a May 30 Augusta report credited the wife and a grandson. The May 29 dispatches placed the supposed lynching on the night of May 28, while the later Augusta account put the rumored lynching on Friday night.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Leroy Gibbons
bases: A mob seized Leroy Gibbons from a guard, put a rope around his neck in a swamp and whipped his wife to force a confession to a killing; he escaped alive (A2, A7, A8).

A group the papers call a mob, acting without authority on an accusation of murder, put a rope around Gibbons's neck and whipped his wife, but Gibbons escaped and no one was killed (A2, A7, A8); this was an attempted lynching.

Separate Augusta and Louisville dispatches agree that Gibbons was seized on the murder accusation, his wife was beaten into accusing him, and he escaped and surrendered (A2, A5, A8), and the Black-press Plaindealer gives the same core account (A13).

framing.detail: First AP reports headlined 'Has Probably Been Lynched' and 'Confessed That His Father Is Murderer', treating Gibbons as Holmes's killer.
Corrections headlined 'Gibbons Really Escaped' and digest lines that Holmes came home uninjured.
Savannah Morning News: 'Lied Under the Lash', Gibbons 'a peaceable old negro' and 'an innocent man'; editorial urges the law take its course.
Deseret Evening News editorial 'A Lynching' calls the attackers 'a band of white ruffians' and lynchers' excuses 'miserable pretenses'.
Plaindealer 'The Danger of Lynching': the 'brutal hope' of the lash and the 'outrage and danger of mob rule'.
